questions.title: Movement lost when the shoulder cannot move forward (protraction)
questions.question: A patient cannot move the shoulder anteriorly, which one of the following movements is lost?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Protrusion is not the standard term used for scapular/shoulder-girdle movement in this direction; the exam and standard anatomical usage reserve it for the mandible.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Retrusion, like protrusion, is a term used for the mandible moving backward, not for the shoulder girdle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Opposition is the thumb pulp meeting the pulp of another digit; it has nothing to do with moving the shoulder forward.
explanations.D: Correct. Protraction is the forward gliding movement of the scapula around the chest wall, carrying the shoulder anteriorly, produced chiefly by serratus anterior and pectoralis minor. Losing the ability to move the shoulder anteriorly is therefore a loss of protraction specifically, distinguishing it from retraction (the opposite, posterior-pulling movement) and from elevation/depression, which move the scapula up or down rather than forward or back. The clinical picture that most classically produces this loss is long thoracic nerve palsy, which paralyses serratus anterior and also causes a winged scapula.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Retraction is the opposite movement, pulling the shoulder girdle backward toward the midline, produced by the rhomboids and middle trapezius; losing it would prevent backward movement, not forward movement.

questions.learning_objective: Movement lost when the shoulder cannot move forward (protraction)

questions.title: Movement lost when the thumb cannot meet the other fingers (opposition)
questions.question: A patient cannot move the thumb to meet each of the other four fingers, which one of the following movements is lost?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Abduction of the thumb moves it away from the palm in a plane perpendicular to it; it does not by itself bring the thumb pulp to meet the other digits.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Adduction brings the thumb back toward the index finger in the plane of the palm; it is one component of opposition but not the composite movement being described.
explanations.C: Correct. Opposition is the composite movement, unique to the thumb, that combines abduction, flexion and medial rotation at the carpometacarpal joint so the thumb pulp can meet the pulp of each of the other four fingers in turn. It is what makes precision (pinch) grip possible, and its motor supply is the median nerve via the muscles of the thenar eminence, chiefly opponens pollicis. Loss of opposition, as in low median nerve palsy, is disabling because it removes the hand's pincer function even though the individual movements of flexion, abduction and adduction may each still be intact on their own.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Reposition is the return movement from opposition back to the resting, unopposed position of the thumb — the opposite of what is being lost here.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Flexion alone bends the thumb across the palm without the rotation component; flexion is only one part of the composite movement of opposition, not opposition itself.

questions.learning_objective: Movement lost when the thumb cannot meet the other fingers (opposition)

questions.title: Term correctly describing supination
questions.question: Which one of the following terms is correct regarding supination?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Abduction moves a limb away from the midline in a coronal plane; supination is a rotational movement of the forearm, not a movement away from the midline.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Adduction moves a limb toward the midline; it does not describe the rotation of the radius that occurs in supination.
explanations.C: Correct. Supination turns the palm to face anteriorly (in the anatomical position) or upward, and it is achieved by lateral (external) rotation of the radius around the ulna at the proximal and distal radio-ulnar joints, carrying the radius from its pronated, crossed position back to lie parallel with the ulna. Biceps brachii is the most powerful supinator when the elbow is flexed, assisted by supinator itself at any elbow angle. Describing supination as a lateral rotation of the radius is the anatomically precise way to classify what is otherwise a named, special movement of the forearm.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Medial rotation of the radius is what produces pronation, turning the palm to face posteriorly or downward — the opposite of supination.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Circumduction is a compound, circular sequence of flexion-abduction-extension-adduction seen at ball-and-socket or condyloid joints; it is not the movement being asked about here.

questions.learning_objective: Term correctly describing supination

questions.title: Term for the sole of the foot facing outward (eversion)
questions.question: Which one of the following terms is correct if sole of the foot faces outward or laterally?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Dorsiflexion moves the whole foot upward at the ankle joint, bringing the dorsum of the foot toward the shin; it does not turn the sole outward.
explanations.B: Correct. Eversion turns the sole of the foot to face outward (laterally), occurring mainly at the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints, produced chiefly by the peroneus (fibularis) longus and brevis muscles. It is the direct opposite of inversion, and the two are frequently combined with dorsiflexion or plantarflexion in the compound movements of pronation and supination of the foot. Ankle sprains most often occur in forced inversion rather than eversion, because the lateral ligaments resisting inversion are weaker than the strong deltoid ligament resisting eversion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Inversion is the opposite movement, turning the sole to face inward (medially), produced chiefly by tibialis anterior and tibialis posterior.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Plantarflexion points the foot downward at the ankle joint, away from the shin; it does not turn the sole to face laterally.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lateral rotation is a term used for whole-limb rotation around a long axis (as at the hip or shoulder), not for the specific foot movement of turning the sole outward.

questions.learning_objective: Term for the sole of the foot facing outward (eversion)

questions.title: Term for limb movement away from the midline (abduction)
questions.question: Movement of the limb away from the midline of the body is called which one of the followings?

explanations.A: Correct. Abduction is defined as movement of a limb, or part of a limb, away from the midline of the body (or, for digits, away from the axis of the hand or foot), typically occurring in the coronal plane at joints such as the shoulder and hip. It is paired with, and is the direct opposite of, adduction, which returns the limb toward the midline. This midline-referenced definition is the standard anatomical convention used consistently across all limb movement terminology.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Protraction describes a forward-gliding movement, most often of the mandible or the scapula, not movement of a limb away from the midline.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Flexion decreases the angle at a joint, usually moving a part anteriorly (or posteriorly at the knee); it is not defined by distance from the midline.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Extension increases the angle at a joint, the opposite of flexion; like flexion, it is not a midline-referenced movement.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Adduction is the opposite of abduction — movement of a limb toward the midline of the body — not away from it.

questions.learning_objective: Term for limb movement away from the midline (abduction)

questions.title: Movements performed by the wrist joint
questions.question: Which of the following movements are done by the wrist joint:

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own. Flexion is indeed one movement the wrist performs, but it is not the only one, so it is not the single best answer when a more complete option is available.
explanations.B: Incorrect on its own. Extension is also a genuine wrist movement, but again only one of several, so it under-states what the joint can do.
explanations.C: Incorrect on its own. Adduction (ulnar deviation) is a real wrist movement, but selecting it alone omits the other movements the joint performs.
explanations.D: Incorrect on its own. Abduction (radial deviation) is likewise a genuine wrist movement, but naming it alone is incomplete.
explanations.E: Correct. The wrist (radiocarpal) joint is a condyloid (ellipsoid) synovial joint, and condyloid joints characteristically allow two degrees of freedom: flexion-extension and abduction-adduction, plus circumduction as their combination. All four listed movements — flexion, extension, adduction (ulnar deviation) and abduction (radial deviation) — are therefore genuinely performed at the wrist, which is exactly why "all of the above" is the single best answer rather than any one movement alone.

questions.learning_objective: Movements performed by the wrist joint

questions.title: Bone developing by intramembranous ossification (skull vault)
questions.question: Which of the following bones develops by intra-membranous ossification?

explanations.A: Correct. The flat bones of the skull vault (the roof bones, such as the frontal and parietal bones) ossify by the intramembranous route: mesenchymal cells condense directly into osteoblasts within a fibrous membrane, without an intervening cartilage model. This is why the vault bones can grow rapidly to accommodate the expanding brain and why the fontanelles (unossified membrane) persist at birth between adjacent vault bones. It contrasts with endochondral ossification, which first lays down a hyaline cartilage model that is later replaced by bone, as happens in essentially every long bone of the limbs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The radius is a typical long bone of the limb and ossifies endochondrally, from a cartilage model, not intramembranously.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The carpal bones are short bones that also ossify endochondrally from cartilage models, each developing its own secondary ossification centre after birth.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The metacarpals are miniature long bones and, like other limb bones, ossify endochondrally rather than intramembranously.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The phalanges are likewise miniature long bones that ossify endochondrally, each from its own cartilage model.

questions.learning_objective: Bone developing by intramembranous ossification (skull vault)

questions.title: Structure responsible for a long bone growing in width (periosteum)
questions.question: Growth of bone in width is due to activity of which one of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The epiphysis is the bony end of a long bone; it is not itself the tissue layer responsible for widening the shaft.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The diaphysis is the shaft of the long bone — the structure that gets wider, not the tissue that makes it widen.
explanations.C: Correct. A long bone widens by appositional growth: osteoblasts in the deep, osteogenic layer of the periosteum lay down new bone on the outer surface of the shaft, while osteoclasts on the inner (endosteal) surface resorb bone to enlarge the medullary cavity, together increasing the bone's diameter without a cartilage intermediate. This periosteal widening happens throughout growth alongside, but independently of, the epiphyseal-plate lengthening mechanism, and it continues in a slower form throughout adult life as part of normal bone remodelling.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The metaphysis is the transitional, actively remodelling zone of the shaft just deep to the epiphyseal plate; it is where longitudinal growth is converted into mature bone, not the site responsible for widening.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The epiphyseal cartilage (growth plate) is responsible for growth in length, not in width — that is precisely the distinction this question and its paired question are testing.

questions.learning_objective: Structure responsible for a long bone growing in width (periosteum)

questions.title: Structure responsible for a long bone growing in length (epiphyseal cartilage)
questions.question: Growth of bone in length is due to activity of which one of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The epiphysis is the ossified end of the bone on the far side of the growth plate; it does not itself generate new length.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The metaphysis is where cartilage produced by the growth plate is being converted into bone; it is the site of ossification of new length, not the site that generates it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The periosteum is responsible for growth in width by appositional new bone formation, not for growth in length.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The diaphysis is the shaft that is being lengthened; it is not itself the source of new growth.
explanations.E: Correct. A long bone lengthens at its epiphyseal (growth) plate of hyaline cartilage, where chondrocytes proliferate and undergo an ordered sequence of columnar arrangement, hypertrophy and calcification before being replaced by bone at the metaphysis — a process called endochondral ossification. The epiphyseal plate at one end of a bone typically closes (ossifies) earlier than the plate at the other end, and the end that keeps growing longer, because its plate closes later, is called the growing end of that bone. Growth in length stops permanently once both epiphyseal plates fuse with the diaphysis at the end of puberty, under hormonal control that occurs about two years earlier in females than in males.

questions.learning_objective: Structure responsible for a long bone growing in length (epiphyseal cartilage)

questions.title: Classification of the tarsal bones (short bones)
questions.question: The tarsal bones are:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Irregular bones are ones with complex shapes that fit none of the other categories, such as the vertebrae or the bones of the face; the tarsals have a simpler, roughly cuboidal shape.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Flat bones are thin, plate-like bones such as the skull vault or the sternum, built for protection or broad muscle attachment; the tarsals are not flat.
explanations.C: Correct. The tarsal bones (talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid and the three cuneiforms) are classified as short bones: roughly cuboidal bones, similar in length, breadth and thickness, that consist of a thin outer shell of compact bone surrounding a core of spongy (cancellous) bone. This shape and internal architecture is well suited to their role of transmitting and absorbing load through the foot while still allowing a degree of gliding movement between adjacent bones. The carpal bones of the wrist share the same classification for the same functional reason.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Modified long bone" is not the standard classification for the tarsals; that description is used instead for atypical long bones such as the clavicle.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Short long bone" (or miniature long bone) describes small bones that still have a shaft and epiphyses, such as the metacarpals and phalanges — a different shape from the tarsals, which have no shaft.

questions.learning_objective: Classification of the tarsal bones (short bones)

questions.title: Which bone is not a typical long bone (metacarpal)
questions.question: All of the following are typical long bones except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is typical). The fibula has a shaft with an epiphysis ossifying separately at each end, satisfying the definition of a typical long bone.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is typical). The radius likewise has a diaphysis with a proximal and a distal epiphysis, each with its own secondary ossification centre, so it is a typical long bone.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is typical). The ulna also has a shaft with two separately-ossifying epiphyses (proximal, at the olecranon, and distal, at the head), so it too is typical.
explanations.D: Correct. A typical long bone has a diaphysis (shaft) with an epiphysis, and its own secondary ossification centre, at each end. The metacarpal bones instead have only one epiphysis — at their distal (head) end — with the proximal (base) end fusing directly with the shaft without a separate ossification centre, which is exactly what makes them "miniature" or "short" long bones rather than typical ones. The same single-epiphysis pattern is shared by the metatarsals and the phalanges.
explanations.E: Incorrect. One of the listed bones (the metacarpal) is indeed the exception, so "none of the above" is not correct.

questions.learning_objective: Which bone is not a typical long bone (metacarpal)

questions.title: Which bone is a miniature long bone (metacarpal)
questions.question: Which of the following is miniature long bone?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The clavicle is classified as a modified long bone: it has no medullary cavity and ossifies partly intramembranously, an atypical pattern of its own rather than the miniature/single-epiphysis pattern.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The humerus is a typical long bone, with a shaft and a separately-ossifying epiphysis at each end.
explanations.C: Correct. The metacarpal bones are miniature (short) long bones: like a typical long bone they have a diaphysis, but unlike a typical long bone they possess only a single epiphysis, at the distal (head) end, while the proximal (base) end fuses to the shaft without its own secondary ossification centre. The metatarsals and phalanges share this same single-epiphysis, small-scale long-bone pattern, which is why all three are grouped together as miniature long bones.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The patella is a sesamoid bone, embedded within the quadriceps tendon, and is not classified as any type of long bone.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The carpal bones are short bones (cuboidal, with a compact shell around cancellous bone), not long bones of any kind.

questions.learning_objective: Which bone is a miniature long bone (metacarpal)

questions.title: Long bone with only one epiphysis (miniature long bone)
questions.question: A long bone having only one epiphysis is called which one of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A typical long bone is defined by having an epiphysis, with its own secondary ossification centre, at each end — two epiphyses, not one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A modified long bone (such as the clavicle) is atypical for other reasons — absent medullary cavity, partly intramembranous ossification — not specifically defined by having a single epiphysis.
explanations.C: Correct. A miniature (or short) long bone still has the diaphysis characteristic of a long bone, but only one epiphysis, at one end, while the other end fuses to the shaft without a separate ossification centre. The metacarpals, metatarsals and phalanges are the classic examples of this single-epiphysis pattern, distinguishing them from the two-epiphysis typical long bones such as the femur or humerus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Short bones (such as the carpals and tarsals) have no shaft or epiphyses at all — they are not long bones of any kind, so the epiphysis count does not apply to them.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Irregular bones (such as the vertebrae) also have no long-bone shaft/epiphysis structure to count.

questions.learning_objective: Long bone with only one epiphysis (miniature long bone)

questions.title: Type of the first carpometacarpal joint (saddle)
questions.question: The type of first carpometacarpal joint is which one of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A hinge joint (such as the elbow or interphalangeal joints) allows movement in one plane only; the thumb's CMC joint moves in more than one plane.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An ellipsoid (condyloid) joint, such as the wrist, allows flexion-extension and abduction-adduction but not the free axial rotation that the thumb CMC joint has.
explanations.C: Correct. The first carpometacarpal (CMC) joint, between the trapezium and the base of the first metacarpal, is a saddle joint: each articular surface is convex in one direction and concave in the perpendicular direction, like a horse's saddle and rider. This shape gives the joint two degrees of freedom (flexion-extension and abduction-adduction) plus enough axial rotation for their combination to produce opposition, which is exactly the biaxial-with-extra-rotation mobility the thumb needs and no other CMC joint (all plane joints) has.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The other carpometacarpal joints (2nd-5th) are plane synovial joints, allowing only limited gliding; the thumb's CMC joint is the one exception, built for far greater mobility.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A pivot joint (such as the proximal radio-ulnar joint) allows rotation around a single longitudinal axis only, which does not match the thumb CMC joint's biaxial-plus-rotation mobility.

questions.learning_objective: Type of the first carpometacarpal joint (saddle)

questions.title: Joint type of the elbow (hinge)
questions.question: To which type of joints the elbow belongs?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ellipsoid joints, like the wrist, allow movement in two perpendicular planes; the elbow is limited to one plane.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Saddle joints, like the thumb CMC joint, allow biaxial movement plus rotation; the elbow proper does not.
explanations.C: Correct. The elbow (humero-ulnar) joint is a uniaxial hinge (ginglymus) synovial joint, permitting flexion and extension only, around a single transverse axis passing roughly through the trochlea of the humerus. Movement is confined to this one plane because the trochlear notch of the ulna closely embraces the trochlea, and strong collateral ligaments on each side prevent side-to-side or rotatory movement at this specific articulation. The separate humero-radial and proximal radio-ulnar joints, which do allow rotation (pronation/supination), are anatomically distinct joints sharing the same joint capsule, which is why the "elbow region" as a whole can rotate even though the hinge joint itself cannot.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A pivot joint, like the proximal radio-ulnar joint, allows rotation around one longitudinal axis; the humero-ulnar hinge joint does not permit rotation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A plane joint allows only small gliding movements between flat or near-flat surfaces, which does not describe the elbow's large flexion-extension range.

questions.learning_objective: Joint type of the elbow (hinge)

questions.title: Axis of movement at hinge synovial joints (transverse)
questions.question: In hing synovial joints, the movements occur around an axis:

explanations.A: Correct. Hinge (ginglymus) joints, such as the elbow, knee and interphalangeal joints, are uniaxial: movement (flexion and extension) occurs around a single transverse axis, running roughly side to side through the joint, which is why hinge joints move in only one plane (like a door on its hinge). This transverse-axis, one-plane restriction is the defining mechanical feature that distinguishes a hinge joint from a pivot joint (which rotates around a longitudinal axis) or a biaxial/multiaxial joint.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A longitudinal axis is the axis used by pivot joints (such as the proximal radio-ulnar joint) for rotation, not by hinge joints.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An anteroposterior axis is used by joints that abduct/adduct in the coronal plane, not by uniaxial hinge joints.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This combines the correct transverse axis with the incorrect longitudinal axis; a hinge joint uses only the transverse axis, not both.
explanations.E: Incorrect. This combines two axes neither of which, alone or together, describes the single transverse axis of a hinge joint.

questions.learning_objective: Axis of movement at hinge synovial joints (transverse)

questions.title: Type of the knee joint (modified hinge)
questions.question: The type of the knee joint is which one of the following?

explanations.A: Correct. The knee joint is classified as a modified hinge (ginglymus) joint. Its predominant movement is uniaxial flexion-extension, like a simple hinge, but it departs from a pure hinge because it also permits a small amount of medial and lateral rotation when the knee is flexed, and because during the last few degrees of extension the femur rotates medially on the tibia (or the tibia laterally on the femur) to "screw home" and lock the fully extended knee. This combination of a dominant hinge action with a secondary rotatory component is exactly why it is called "modified" rather than a pure hinge joint.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An ellipsoid joint (such as the wrist) allows biaxial movement in two perpendicular planes without significant axial rotation, which does not match the knee's hinge-plus-rotation pattern.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A ball-and-socket joint (such as the shoulder or hip) allows movement in all three planes plus free rotation, far more mobility than the knee has.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A saddle joint (such as the thumb CMC joint) has reciprocally curved surfaces giving biaxial movement plus rotation from a different mechanism than the knee's screw-home mechanism.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A pivot joint (such as the proximal radio-ulnar joint) allows rotation around a single longitudinal axis only, with no flexion-extension, which is not how the knee moves.

questions.learning_objective: Type of the knee joint (modified hinge)

questions.title: Type of the metacarpophalangeal joints (condyloid)
questions.question: Which is the type of the metacarpophalangeal joints?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A plane joint allows only small gliding movements between flat surfaces, far less mobility than the MCP joints have.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A hinge joint is uniaxial (flexion-extension only); the MCP joints also abduct and adduct, which a hinge joint cannot do.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A pivot joint allows rotation around a single longitudinal axis only, which does not describe the MCP joint's movement.
explanations.D: Correct. The metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints are condyloid (ellipsoid) synovial joints: the convex, ellipsoid head of the metacarpal fits into the shallow, oval concavity of the base of the proximal phalanx. This shape gives them two degrees of freedom — flexion-extension (the larger range) and abduction-adduction (the smaller range, at the fingers, that lets the fingers spread and close) — plus a limited element of circumduction from combining the two, exactly the mobility profile expected of a condyloid joint.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A syndesmosis is a fibrous (not synovial) joint in which bones are united by a ligament or interosseous membrane, such as the distal tibiofibular joint; the MCP joints are freely mobile synovial joints, not fibrous ones.

questions.title: Which is not a type of fibrous joint (synchondrosis)
questions.question: All of the following are types of fibrous joints except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is fibrous). A suture, such as those between the skull vault bones, is a fibrous joint in which the bones are united by a thin layer of dense fibrous tissue.
explanations.B: Correct. Synchondrosis is a primary cartilaginous joint, not a fibrous one: the bones are united by hyaline cartilage (as at an epiphyseal plate or the first costochondral joint), typically a temporary joint that itself ossifies once growth is complete. Fibrous joints, by contrast, unite bones with dense fibrous connective tissue and include sutures, gomphoses and syndesmoses; grouping synchondrosis among them is the classic trap this question is testing, since it belongs instead in the cartilaginous-joint category (alongside symphyses, which are secondary cartilaginous joints).
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is fibrous). A gomphosis is the fibrous joint form of a tooth in its bony socket, held by the periodontal ligament — a peg-and-socket fibrous joint.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is fibrous). A syndesmosis, such as the distal tibiofibular joint or the interosseous membranes of the forearm and leg, unites bones with a ligament or fibrous membrane, allowing a small amount of movement.
explanations.E: Incorrect. One option (synchondrosis) is indeed the exception, so "none of the above" is not correct.

questions.title: Type of joint between the glenoid cavity and the head of the humerus (ball and socket)
questions.question: The type of the joint between glenoid cavity and the head of the humerus is:

explanations.A: Correct. The glenohumeral (shoulder) joint, between the shallow glenoid cavity of the scapula and the large spherical head of the humerus, is a ball-and-socket synovial joint — the most mobile joint in the body. Its multiaxial mobility (flexion-extension, abduction-adduction, medial-lateral rotation and circumduction, all combined) comes directly from the spherical head articulating within a socket, at the cost of stability, which is why the shoulder relies heavily on the rotator cuff muscles and the glenoid labrum for support and is the most commonly dislocated large joint in the body.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A condyloid joint (such as the wrist or MCP joints) allows two-plane movement without free axial rotation, far less mobility than the ball-and-socket shoulder joint.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A pivot joint allows rotation around one longitudinal axis only, not the full multiaxial movement the shoulder has.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A saddle joint (such as the thumb CMC joint) has reciprocally curved, not spherical, surfaces, and does not match the ball-and-socket shape of the glenohumeral joint.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Ball and socket is indeed the correct classification, so "none of the above" does not apply.

questions.title: Characteristics of synovial joints (which is not one)
questions.question: All are characteristic of synovial joints except :

options.B: A capsule binds the articulating bones
options.C: The articular ends of bone are covered by synovial membrane

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is characteristic). A synovial joint, by definition, has a joint cavity — a fluid-filled space between the two articulating bones — which is one of its defining features.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is characteristic). A fibrous joint capsule, continuous with the periosteum of each bone, encloses and binds every synovial joint.
explanations.C: Correct. The articular (bearing) surfaces of the bone ends in a synovial joint are covered by hyaline articular cartilage, not by synovial membrane. Synovial membrane instead lines the inner surface of the joint capsule and any non-articular internal surfaces, secreting the lubricating synovial fluid into the joint cavity — but it specifically stops short of, and does not cover, the load-bearing cartilage itself, which is exactly the distinction this question is testing.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is characteristic). Some synovial joints (such as the knee or temporomandibular joint) contain an intra-articular disc or meniscus of fibrocartilage, which can be present as a normal feature.
explanations.E: Incorrect (it is characteristic). Free mobility is the hallmark that distinguishes synovial joints from the far more restricted fibrous and cartilaginous joints.

questions.learning_objective: Characteristics of synovial joints (which is not one)

questions.title: System comprising all hormone-producing glands (endocrine)
questions.question: The system which consists of all glands that produce hormones is which one of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The nervous system communicates by electrical impulses and neurotransmitters released at synapses, not by hormones released into the bloodstream.
explanations.B: Correct. The endocrine system is defined as the collection of ductless glands (such as the pituitary, thyroid, adrenal glands and pancreas islets) that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream to act on distant target tissues, rather than through a duct as exocrine glands do. This distinguishes it from the nervous system, which is the body's other principal communication and control system but signals electrically and locally rather than chemically and at a distance, and the two systems together are often studied as the neuroendocrine axis because of how closely they interact (for example, the hypothalamus controlling the pituitary).
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cardiovascular system transports blood, oxygen and nutrients around the body; while it carries hormones to their targets, it is not itself composed of hormone-producing glands.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The digestive system's primary role is breaking down and absorbing food; although some digestive organs (such as the pancreas) have endocrine components, the system as a whole is not defined by hormone production.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The respiratory system's role is gas exchange; it is not composed of hormone-producing glands.

questions.title: Second movement in shoulder circumduction (abduction)
questions.question: The second movement that occurs during shoulder circumduction is:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the second step. Flexion is the first movement in the conventional circumduction sequence at the shoulder, not the second.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the second step. Extension is the third movement in the sequence, following abduction, not the second.
explanations.C: Correct. Circumduction is a compound movement in which the limb describes a cone, produced by a continuous, sequential combination of the joint's other movements rather than by any independent motion of its own. At the shoulder the conventional teaching sequence runs flexion, then abduction, then extension, then adduction (returning to the start), so abduction — carrying the arm out to the side after the initial forward flexion — is the second movement in that cycle.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the second step. Adduction is the fourth and final movement in the sequence, completing the circle, not the second.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Medial rotation is not one of the four component movements of the classic circumduction sequence at all; circumduction is built from flexion, abduction, extension and adduction.

questions.learning_objective: Second movement in shoulder circumduction (abduction)

questions.title: Circulation connecting two capillary beds (portal)
questions.question: Which of the following circulations connects two capillary beds:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The systemic circulation runs from the left ventricle, through one arterial-to-capillary-to-venous circuit across the whole body, to the right atrium — a single capillary bed in series, not two.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pulmonary circulation runs from the right ventricle through the lungs' capillary bed to the left atrium — again a single capillary bed, not two in series.
explanations.C: Correct. A portal circulation is defined precisely by connecting two capillary (or sinusoidal) beds in series via a portal vein, without an intervening pass back through the heart. The hepatic portal system is the classic example: blood from the capillary beds of the stomach, spleen, pancreas and intestines drains into the portal vein, which carries it to a second capillary bed — the liver sinusoids — before it finally leaves by the hepatic veins. This two-beds-in-series arrangement is what allows the liver to process nutrient- and toxin-laden blood from the gut before it re-joins the general systemic circulation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Only the portal circulation has this two-capillary-bed-in-series property; the systemic and pulmonary circulations each have only one capillary bed, so "all of the above" over-states it.
explanations.E: Incorrect. One of the listed circulations (portal) does connect two capillary beds, so "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Circulation connecting two capillary beds (portal)
